input: The picture that emerges from the two lifetime reports is, at first sight, a rather confusing one, because the two groups appear to contradict one another flatly about how long the benchmark material can be expected to last. A closer look, however, suggests that the disagreement may be more apparent than real, since the two groups did not in fact age the benchmark material under the same conditions at all. One of the groups cycled the benchmark material using a dry feed and regenerated it under relatively gentle conditions that the material is known to tolerate well, whereas the other group deliberately worked with a humid feed and a considerably more aggressive regeneration, and the shorter lifetime it reports is therefore, to a significant extent, a reflection of that harsher duty rather than a property of the material alone. It has to be remembered that, for this class of materials, lifetime is intimately bound up with the cycling duty: the humidity of the feed determines the water load that the pores are required to surrender at every regeneration, and the severity of the regeneration determines how much of the framework each individual cycle consumes. It follows that a lifetime measured under one duty can only really be transferred to another duty when the two duties correspond in precisely these respects. The preference that emerges is accordingly a limited one: for a dry feed combined with the milder style of regeneration, the value reported by the first group is the more trustworthy guide, because its test reproduces the loads that govern the loss of capacity, whereas for humid service it is the second group's figure, lower though it is, that the design should carry. Neither report, it should be said, actually provides a lifetime at a declared cycling count with the feed humidity and the regeneration severity both stated alongside it.
target: The conflict between the two lifetime reports is narrower than the reported values suggest, because the two groups did not age the benchmark material under the same conditions. The benchmark material is the same in both studies; the synthesis route and the activation are reported in the same terms, so the difference in outcome is not explained by the specimen. One group cycled the benchmark material under a dry feed and regenerated at a severity the material tolerates well; the other group worked with a humid feed and a harder regeneration, and its shorter lifetime is a record of that duty as much as of the material. Lifetime in this class of materials is a property of the cycling duty: the feed humidity sets the water load the pores must give up at each regeneration, and the regeneration severity sets how much of the framework each cycle costs. The two reports also agree on more than they dispute: the material class, the benchmark specimen, and the direction in which harsher duty shortens life are common ground between them. A lifetime measured under either duty transfers to a new duty only where the two duties match in those respects. On that basis the preference here is limited: for a dry feed with regeneration of the milder kind, the first group's value is the better guide, because its test reproduces the loads that govern the loss of capacity. The preference does not extend to humid service, where the second group's conditions are the closer match and its value, though lower, is the one the design should carry. What neither report supplies is a lifetime under a stated cycling count with the feed humidity and the regeneration severity both declared alongside it, and until such a report exists the comparison stays where the present section leaves it, on the match of conditions rather than on the standing of either group.
